Pi

|View as Markdown|Agent setup

Pi ↗︎ is a minimal, extensible agent harness. The Agents SDK provides first-class support for building agents using the Pi harness, and this page shows how to run Pi Durable ↗︎ in a Cloudflare Durable Object with PiHarness from the Agents SDK.

Pi runs the agent loop: the transcript, the inbox of follow-ups and steers, model calls, tools, retries, and crash recovery. PiHarness gives Pi storage in the Durable Object's SQLite database, and wakes the object when Pi has work to finish.

To start from a complete app, deploy the Pi harness example ↗︎. It streams sessions to a browser UI over WebSockets, and gives Pi a durable filesystem and JavaScript execution from @cloudflare/computer.

How it works

PiHarness is a new "Lifecycle capability" provided by the Cloudflare Agents SDK. Pi Durable provides the agent harness and the Lifecycle is responsible for keeping the agent running in the Durable Object. The Lifecycle is a core concept in the Agents SDK ensuring that long-running work can run in a Durable Object, surviving restarts, crashes, and network issues. A Lifecycle capability is a reusable piece of a Durable Object that the Lifecycle starts and gives SQLite storage and a durable job queue. PiHarness uses them in two ways:

  • Storage. Pi keeps its transcripts, inbox, and tasks in its own tables in the object's SQLite database. The table names start with pi_, so they do not collide with your own tables.
  • Wake-up. Pi's scheduler runs in memory, and an evicted object has none. PiHarness schedules one Lifecycle job for the object, driven by Pi's wake(). The job keeps a heartbeat while Pi works, is due when Pi's next sleeping task wakes, and completes when Pi has nothing to do. If the object is evicted mid-run, the job's alarm restarts it, Pi reopens its storage, and the run continues.

PiHarness does not choose how clients reach a session. It gives you a watch of each session's state, and you send it over WebSockets, HTTP, or RPC.

Install

Install agents with Pi Durable, Pi AI, Pi Schema, and Chord:

npm i agents @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai @earendil-works/pi-schema @earendil-works/chord
yarn add agents @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai @earendil-works/pi-schema @earendil-works/chord
pnpm add agents @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai @earendil-works/pi-schema @earendil-works/chord
bun add agents @earendil-works/pi-durable @earendil-works/pi-ai @earendil-works/pi-schema @earendil-works/chord

The Pi packages are optional peer dependencies of agents, at ~1.6.0. Pi Durable is experimental and its API can change in minor releases, so each agents release supports one Pi minor version. Install the versions your package manager resolves for agents.

Agents SDK 0.34.0 and later support Pi 1.6. A new Pi minor version can store conversations in a format the previous one cannot read. After a conversation runs on Pi 1.6, rolling your Worker back to an Agents SDK version on Pi 1.5 blocks its tool calls and model requests, because Pi 1.6 stores them in versions that Pi 1.5 does not run. Roll forward to fix a bad deploy instead.

The agents/models/pi-ai entry point supports AI Gateway and Workers AI models, so you can get started with Cloudflare models right away or use your existing Pi AI provider. The examples on this page use Workers AI through the AI binding and the Pi AI model provider. Add the binding and a SQLite-backed Durable Object to your Wrangler configuration:

Create the agent

PiHarness is a Lifecycle capability, so it runs on a plain Durable Object. Open Pi's Harness in a factory, install a Lifecycle on the object, and add the harness to it:

The harness factory receives storage, Pi's storage over the object's SQLite database, context, a background context for opening Pi, and onWake, so the object can hibernate while Pi's tasks sleep. Everything else that Harness.open() takes is yours to build in the factory: models, the registry of tools and prompt sections, settings, env, and onReport.

The factory runs inside the object's startup, before any session is used, and again whenever the harness reopens Pi after a storage error (refer to Recovery). Keep it safe to run more than once. If it throws, the operation that started it fails, and the next operation tries again. Every PiHarness operation waits for startup, so a call that arrives over RPC before startup does not open Pi on its own.

Options

Option Description
harness Required. Receives { storage, context, onWake } and returns Pi's Harness, usually from Harness.open(). Pass onWake on to Harness.open().
defaults What a new session starts with: model, a Pi AI Model such as ai("@cf/..."), thinkingLevel, and maxTurns, the most tool rounds one run takes. Change one session's model later with session.setModel().

Without a model, a session's prompts end unanswered until you set one. A run that reaches maxTurns runs that round's tools, then ends unanswered with reason turn_limit. Like the other defaults, maxTurns applies to new sessions only. Changing it does not change sessions that already exist. Without it, a run takes as many tool rounds as the model asks for.

Settings for the whole harness go in Pi's settings, passed to Harness.open(). For example, Pi retries a failed model request 3 times by default, and settings: { retry: { maxRetries: 2, baseDelayMs: 500 } } changes that. compaction and toolExecution set how Pi compacts long transcripts and runs a round's tools.

Add tools and a system prompt

Both tools and system prompt sections are provided to the Pi Harness via extensions. A Pi extension is a plain object with a name, tools, and sections. Install it on the registry you open Pi with:

For more information on creating and configuring extensions, including skills and replay safety, refer to Extensions.

Send prompts

harness.prompt() submits to the root session and waits for the answer. It returns the final assistant text, the status, and the session's transcript as messages.

For long runs, submit and wait separately. submit() returns once Pi has durably stored the input, before the model runs. wait() returns the result when Pi finishes:

An operationId makes a submission idempotent. Submitting the same id again returns the same operation with accepted: false. Use an id that survives your own retries, such as an inbound event id.

A submission made while the session is running is queued and answered after the current run, as its own run. Set whenBusy: "steer", or call session.steer(), to join the running work after its current tool round instead. Set whenIdle: "reject" so an idle session refuses the input with Pi's ConversationIdle instead of starting a run. With whenBusy: "steer" as well, the input joins the running work or is refused, without racing the end of the run.

Aborting a session withdraws the inputs queued in it. Set onAbort: "keep" on input that its sender cannot send again, such as another agent's message, and the input stays queued through an abort instead. The next input, continue(), or reset() runs it first. A kept steer waits for the next input or continue(). abort(operationId) still withdraws it.

harness.pending() lists submissions Pi has not finished, with their status: queued or running.

Label input the user did not type

Pi records every submitted input as a pi.user entry, as if the user typed it. Your code often submits input of its own, such as a prompt from a scheduled job, a webhook payload, or the outcome of an approval. To record where that input came from, pass entry with a kind of your own and any data you want to keep with it:

The model sees no difference: it still gets the text as a user message. Only the transcript changes. The input is stored with your kind and data instead of pi.user, and messages(), watch(), and entries() return both, so your UI can show it differently, for example as "Approved by ben" rather than as something the user said. Pi reserves kinds that start with pi., so use a prefix of your own, such as app..

The kind is a label, not a permission. It records what your code said the input was, and nothing checks it. The model reads the input as if the user wrote it, so do not put anything in it that you would not let the user send.

Inputs queued behind a failed run

A run fails with model_error when the model errors and Pi does not retry it, or the error outlasts Pi's retries. It fails with no_model when the session has no usable model, and with turn_limit when it reaches defaults.maxTurns. The run's own submission settles unanswered with that reason. Once you have fixed the cause, call session.continue() to answer the transcript as it is, without a new message. Pi's settings.afterFailedRun decides what happens to the submissions queued behind it:

Value Result
keep (default) pending() lists them as queued, and wait() keeps waiting. The next submit() runs them first, in order, then the new input. The next reset() runs them too.
continue The next run starts with them. If the cause persists, such as a missing model, each one fails in its own run.
withdraw wait() returns { status: "unanswered", reason: "run_failed" }, and pending() no longer lists them.

Set it in the factory:

With keep, the kept submissions are not work for Pi, so the object can hibernate until the next submit() or reset(). Pass a signal to wait() if a caller should not wait that long. To withdraw a kept submission, call abort(operationId). session.abort() with no id withdraws every kept submission too, apart from those submitted with onAbort: "keep".

Work with sessions

A session is a Pi conversation. The root session has the id "1". The harness methods take an optional session option, and harness.session(id) returns a handle for one session:

Method Description
submit(input, options) Durably submit input with operationId, whenBusy, whenIdle, onAbort, entry, or notify. Returns a receipt.
continue(options) Start a run on the transcript as it is, without a new message. Only an idle session takes one. Takes operationId and notify.
prompt(input, options) Submit and wait for the answer and the updated transcript.
steer(input) Submit with whenBusy: "steer".
wait(operationId, signal) Wait for an operation. Aborting signal stops the wait, not the work.
abort(operationId) Withdraw a queued operation, or abort the run it joined. With no id, abort everything in the session and withdraw its queued inputs, apart from those submitted with onAbort: "keep".
pending() Operations Pi has not settled yet: queued or running.
reset(handoff) Start a new context, optionally from a handoff note. Inputs kept behind a failed run or an abort start a run in it.
setModel(model) Change this session's model to a Pi AI Model, such as ai("@cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017").
messages() The active transcript, as Pi's EntryRecord entries since the newest reset.
watch(window) Pi's view of the session: the newest transcript entries and the session's live state.
entries(query, limit) A page of the session's transcript, including entries before its resets.
busy() Whether the session is running.

sessions.create() makes a new top-level session with the harness defaults. sessions.fork(id) makes a session that sees another's history up to its newest entry. sessions.list() includes sessions that Pi's subagent tools created. harness.signal() delivers a signal to a parked tool call. Refer to Tools that wait.

The harness creates the root session, with defaults, the first time a call works with it, such as prompt(), submit(), messages(), or watch(). Calls that only read around it, such as pending(), busy(), and sessions.list(), do not create it, and sessions.list() does not include the root until it exists. To create the root yourself, with your own configuration or history, call harness.root(). Refer to Seed a session with an existing history.

Session ids are Pi's conversation ids, so you cannot choose them. To give each user or chat its own agent, use one Durable Object per conversation and the root session in each.

session.continue() answers the transcript as it is, for example after a run ended unanswered because the model errored or the run reached maxTurns. A busy session rejects it with Pi's ConversationBusy. A transcript that already ends in an answer has nothing to continue, so the operation settles unanswered with reason nothing_to_answer. Like submit(), it takes an operationId and returns a receipt for wait().

Seed a session with an existing history

To start a session from a chat history your application already has, such as one imported from another system, write the history into the session's transcript in the commit that creates the session. harness.root(), sessions.create(), and sessions.fork() take two options for that:

Option Description
agent Pi's AgentChange, such as instructions or thinkingLevel. For the root and create(), it is applied over defaults. A fork starts with the configuration of the session it forks, and agent is applied over that. A field that is undefined keeps the value underneath, and null clears it.
init Pi's ConversationInit, (tx, conversationId) => .... It runs inside the commit that creates the session, after agent. Append one entry per message with tx.appendEntry(). If it throws, the commit fails and the session is not created.

Use Pi's own entry kinds, so Pi treats the messages as if they had happened in the session: UserEntry for a user message, AssistantEntry for a model message, and ToolResultEntry for a tool result, with an empty diagnostics list. An assistant message needs usage, which Pi sums. An imported message has none, so give it zeros. Its api, provider, and model name the model that wrote it. The example takes them from a model of createAI:

harness.root() returns the root session and created. When the root does not exist yet, root() creates it with agent and init in one commit, and created is true. When the root already exists, because another call used it first or an earlier root() created it, nothing is written, init does not run, and created is false. Call root() before anything else uses the root, and check created instead of assuming the history was written. A root() whose init throws creates nothing, so a later root() can try again.

sessions.create({ agent, init }) and sessions.fork(from, { agent, init }) seed the session they create the same way. A fork's init appends after the history that the fork copies from from.

Watch sessions from clients

session.watch() returns Pi's view of the session: the newest transcript entries, and the session's live state in pi.live, such as the answer being streamed, running tools, and why the last run ended without an answer. Render the first value, then each new one:

To send a session over a socket, send watch.value once, then each change's call.ops. The client applies them to its copy of the view with applyImmutable() from @earendil-works/chord/delta.

live.run is set while the session is running. live.runFailure stays after a failed run until the next run starts, so check live.run === undefined to tell whether the session is idle.

The view holds the newest 50 entries and grows to 100 before its oldest entries leave. Unlike messages(), its entries include those before a reset or compaction: Pi adds the reset or summary entry in place instead of cutting the transcript there. To render a longer transcript, merge each value into Pi's ConversationTranscript, which pages older entries with session.entries(). After a client reconnects, pass the transcript's resume window to session.watch() to get only the entries it missed.

A client that connects mid-run gets the partial answer in its first value. A watch lives in memory. After the object restarts, open a new watch and send its first value again.

The entries in messages() and the view are Pi's transcript entries, not a chat UI format. Map them to what your client renders.

For anything PiHarness does not cover, await harness.pi() returns the opened Pi Harness. Call harness.root() before you reach the root session through it: until the root is first used, Pi's pi.conversation(ROOT_CONVERSATION_ID) returns undefined, and Pi's own pi.root() would create the root without the harness defaults. Deliver signals with harness.signal(), not with pi.signal().

Tools that wait

A Pi tool can park instead of returning a result: it returns { sleep: { signals, until } }, and Pi runs it again when one of the signals arrives or the deadline passes. While the call waits, it holds no invocation, so the Durable Object can hibernate or be evicted. Deliver a signal with harness.signal(), for example from the request that carries a person's answer:

harness.signal() returns Pi's result: delivered, or duplicate, invalid, closed, or not_found when the call did not take the value. It schedules the harness's wake-up job before it hands Pi the value, so if the object dies while the woken call runs, the job's alarm restarts it. Deliver signals through harness.signal(), not through harness.pi().

A tool can also have a cancel() function, which Pi runs when a parked call is aborted, for example to cancel the work it was waiting on. A beforeTool hook can park a call the same way before the call runs, to hold it for an approval, a rate limit, or a budget. Pi runs the hook again each time it reopens, so keep the hook idempotent.

While a call is parked, its run is still going: pending() lists its operation as running, busy() is true, and Pi's pi.live shows the call's slot as sleeping or waiting. For the rules a parking tool follows, refer to Tools that park ↗︎ and Gates before a tool runs ↗︎ in the Pi Durable README.

Wait for a subagent

To have a tool wait for another session's answer, create a session owned by the call, submit to it with notify, and park on Pi's SubmissionSettled signal under the same key. This is Pi's own subagent pattern:

When the child's input settles, Pi delivers the settled record to the call in the same commit, and the tool runs again with it. Because the call owns the child, aborting the parent session stops the child too, and a rerun before the park was stored finds the same child instead of creating another. The requestId makes a rerun find the same submission. If the task to notify has ended or does not exist, the input still settles as usual. session.submit() and session.continue() take the same notify option, for a child session that your own code created.

Recovery

What happens Result
The object is evicted, crashes, or exceeds its memory or CPU limit The wake-up job's next alarm restarts the object, and Pi continues from its last checkpoint.
A deploy happens mid-run Same as a crash. The runtime gives in-flight work 30 seconds, then the alarm restarts the object.
The model was streaming Pi keeps the partial answer it stored. The request counts as a failed attempt under settings.retry, so Pi calls the model again after the retry backoff. With no retry left, the run ends unanswered with reason interrupted.
A tool with replay: "safe" was running Pi runs the tool again.
Any other tool was running Pi does not run it again. The model gets an interrupted result and decides what to do next.

Mark a tool replay: "safe" when running it twice is harmless, such as a read or a whole-file write. Leave other tools unsafe, such as an edit that would fail on text it already replaced, or a call that charges a card.

While Pi has work, the job's heartbeat alarm fires every 30 seconds. A crashed object restarts on the next heartbeat.

While Pi's tasks sleep, such as during a retry backoff, the job is due when the first one wakes. Pi reports when through the onWake callback that the factory passes to Harness.open(), and sets no in-memory timer, so the object can hibernate until then.

A tool parked on a signal with no deadline leaves nothing due, so the job completes, no alarm is set, and the object can hibernate until your code delivers the signal. harness.signal() opens Pi again, schedules the wake-up job, and resumes the call. A restart while a call is parked runs no tool code, even for a tool that is not replay-safe.

Pi shows a streaming answer and running tool output in the view at once, but stores them in batches: with the next change that depends on them, such as the end of the answer, and at the latest after settings.progress.persistWithinMs (default 1,000 ms). A crash mid-stream loses up to that much of the stream. To store every update instead, at the cost of one storage write each, set settings: { progress: { persistWithinMs: 0 } } in Harness.open().

If the factory passes onReport to Harness.open(), Pi reports failures there as one report tagged by kind, such as storage_failed when a storage error closes Pi.

Tasks that keep crashing

A task that keeps crashing the object would restart it forever. Pi ends a task that a crash or eviction cuts off settings.restartLimit times in a row (default 5):

  • A tool call ends with an error result that the model sees, and the run goes on.
  • A model request ends its run, and the run's operations settle unanswered with reason restart_limit.

Either way, the job completes and the object can hibernate. Pi reports the task to onReport as task_interrupted. To run the work again once you have dealt with the cause, call session.continue() or submit it again.

Limitations

  • Approvals. PiHarness has no built-in approval step for tool calls. To hold a call for a person's approval, park it with a beforeTool hook and deliver the answer with harness.signal(). Refer to Tools that wait.
  • Abort and tools. abort() waits until the session is idle. A tool that ignores its abort signal keeps the session busy until it returns.
  • Long model calls. The wake-up job waits inside an alarm invocation, and an alarm invocation runs for up to 15 minutes. The harness hands off to a new alarm every 10 minutes, but one model request that streams for more than 15 minutes can be cut off.
  • Background tasks. Work that Pi runs in the background is checked on each heartbeat, so the harness notices it finish up to 30 seconds late.
  • Graceful eviction. A running session keeps work in flight, so the object does not drain while Pi runs.
  • Session deletion. Pi Durable cannot delete a conversation yet.
